name: Pumice hair removal

lead: Pumice is a light, porous volcanic glass with a rough surface. Rubbed over dry or damp skin, it wears down fine hair and dead skin, leaving the area smoother to look at and touch.

The method is among the oldest grooming techniques on record. It is still used today mainly on feet and calluses, and occasionally on body hair, with no published trials of it as a hair-removal method.

paras: Practitioners rub a damp stone over the area in small strokes, usually in the shower or bath, then moisturise. Hair is worn down rather than cut or pulled, so regrowth tends to feel stubbly and it is repeated as needed.

Over-abrasion can cause redness, scrapes, ingrown hairs and irritation, and a shared or damp stone can harbour bacteria. People with broken, inflamed or sensitive skin are generally advised by clinicians to avoid abrasive tools.

chain: Rough stone abrades hair at the skin surface
Hair is worn down and dead skin is buffed away
angle.text: Pumice removes or thins fine body hair mechanically and buffs the surface skin at the same time. Users choose it as an inexpensive, no-chemical alternative to shaving or waxing for a smooth look.

lead: Pumice hair removal is the practice of rubbing a pumice stone against the skin to wear away body hair. Pumice is an extremely vesicular, rough-textured volcanic glass whose gas-filled structure makes it light and porous, and its surface acts as a mild abrasive.[1] People use it to get a smoother, hair-free look on legs, arms or other areas without a razor or wax.

Historical accounts describe it among the tools used in ancient Egypt for body-hair removal, alongside creams and razors, and a Roman poem from around 100 BC shows pumice being used to rub away dead skin.[1] Today it is far better known as a foot and callus smoother than as a hair-removal tool.[1]
No clinical studies of pumice as a hair-removal method have been published.

paras: Pumice is sold as a stone, often with a handle or on a cord, or as a powder. Its roughness comes from the glassy, bubble-filled structure of the rock.[1]

In ancient Egypt, people removed body hair for reasons including controlling lice and ritual purification, using creams, razors and pumice stones.[1] A Roman poem indicates pumice was used on skin by about 100 BC, and ancient Chinese grooming used it to tidy nails and remove calluses.[1] Powdered pumice also appeared in Roman toothpaste.[1]
Pumice appears in body-care discussions mainly as a mechanical exfoliant and for feet; its use for hair removal is a niche, traditional method.

timeline.event: A Roman poem records pumice used to rub away dead skin.[1]
